title: Interdependent Conditions for Successful Human-AI Delegation
coverNote: Placeholder until the issue cover exists (issue #3)
beats: All four conditions hold. The four gears (the person judging the AI, the AI's confidence dial, the person checking the output, the task's structure) turn together. Tasks flow to the AI, and the person's check catches the wrong results, which flash gold and drop out.

The AI's confidence dial pins at full, so it is equally sure of every answer. Its gear jams, and the jam passes to assessment, then to monitoring, then to the task. The line stops and wrong results pile up under the person.
Only the dial is repaired (coral sparks). It strains but cannot turn, because the monitoring gear is still jammed. Red brackets mark monitoring as the new bottleneck.
All four are repaired together. The gears turn, the line restarts, and the pile of wrong results clears.

title: Simple Is Eco-Friendly (Ryu et al., 2025)
venue: Journal of Advertising (moved here from the chapter, as you asked)
beats: A passerby glances at both posters. The plain poster is easy to take in and lights up; the busy one flickers. The heart goes to the plain poster.
The passerby stops with a goal in mind: a product that works (the bolt). The busy poster now reads as powerful and gives off gold rays, and the heart moves to it.
The goal changes to sustainability (the leaf). The busy poster's ornaments fall off as red waste, the plain poster grows a leaf, and the heart moves back to the plain one.

title: Complexity in Visual Design: Psychological Mechanisms and Practical Implications
beats: One billboard slides from plain to busy and back. A viewer in a hurry, with no time to think, likes it plain: the meter fills green when it is plain and drops to red when it is busy.

Four viewers with four goals watch the same slide. A product that works (the bolt) and enjoyment (the ice cream) like it busy; health (the cross) and sustainability (the leaf) like it plain. Hearts and red crosses swap sides as it changes.
The billboard splits. The bolt and ice cream viewers get the busy version, the cross and leaf viewers get the plain one, and all four meters fill green.

title: AI-Assisted Shopping: On the Preferences of Consumers and Machines
beats: The shopper wants the striped teal product but sends a vague request. The assistant drone scans the shelf, gets pulled toward the familiar gold brand (the coral rings) and puts it in the cart. A poor fit: red X.
Trip after trip brings the familiar brand. Its sales stack up, text about it trains the next model (gold dots flowing back to the drone), its pull grows, and the other products fade.
A detailed request. The drone feels the pull but goes to the lower shelf and brings the striped teal product. A good fit: green check.

title: Cognitive Traps: Detecting AI Agents in Online Research
beats: A person and an AI agent take the same survey. The agent screenshots the screen and reads every word (teal); both tick the right box and get green checks.
The moving robot trap: a gold token steps toward the center of a box. The person puts the next step at the center (green); the agent puts it in a wrong corner (red).

Five more traps flash on the screen (two lines with fins, the cafe wall, ringed circles, planets, colliding circles) while each one's six-slot tally fills: the person 5 green and 1 red, the agent mostly red.
The agent's tally glows coral, a trapdoor drops it, a flag stands where it was, its rows leave the data table, and the monitor turns green.

title: Marketing by Design
beats: Two perfume ads with a practical claim (the gear): one with orderly concentric squares, one with tangled lines. Mouse pointers click; the orderly ad's frame turns coral and its click meter rises higher.
The claim switches to fun (the sparkle). Now the tangled ad gets the coral frame and the taller meter.
A label of exact facts hangs under both ads. The clicks come out even and an equal sign appears between the meters.
Columns of brand value stand on orderly and loose logos, grouped as practical brands and fun brands; the matching pairs stand tallest.

title: Serendipity
beats: In a gallery, the visitor weighs two covered paintings, points at one, it is unveiled, and the visitor likes it: a heart, and the enjoyment slider moves to 60.
The visitor walks down a hallway, turns a corner and comes upon the same painting by chance: coral sparkles, a coral heart, and the slider passes the earlier mark (70).
The same walk ends at an unattractive painting: a red broken heart and the slider falls (43).
A gallery worker carries the painting in, hangs it and points it out to the visitor: a small heart, and the slider stops at about the earlier mark.

title: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance
beats: Two candle listings: one claims an exact burn time (a pin), the other a range (a bracket). A cursor clicks, and most clicks go to the exact claim.

Sponsored labels drop onto both listings and the cursor turns into a magnifying glass. The glass shows the real spread of burn times, which the range covers; the range listing turns green and now gets most of the clicks.
The range is stretched far wider than the real spread. Its empty ends flash red and the clicks split evenly.

title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
beats: Five judges predict a basketball game's total score, from one exact number to a very wide range.
The game is over (knowable): the scoreboard locks on 203. Credibility falls as the intervals widen, and the coral frame picks the exact judge.
The next game is still to come (chance): shots go in or bounce out and the scoreboard runs through possible totals. The credibility bars rise and then fall, and the frame moves to the moderate range.

title: Concealing Prices: How Delayed Price Disclosure Influences Consumer Purchase Decisions
beats: In an upscale store (purple awning, crown), an espresso machine's price tag hangs face down. The shopper's guess in the thought bubble grows from 3 coins to 6.
The tag flips: the real price is 4 coins, below the guess. The extra coins turn green and the machine goes home with the shopper.
The awning turns blue and a sale sign replaces the crown. With the tag hidden, the guess drops to 1 coin.
The tag flips to the same 4 coins, above the guess. The coins turn red and the shopper walks away without the machine.

title: Large language models converge on competitive rationality but diverge on cooperation
beats: The Anthropic, Google and OpenAI marks each sit at a table facing the same opponent. In a competitive game all three land their guesses on the same spots.
In a ten-round cooperation game, the Anthropic model hands a green coin across in most rounds, the Google model in about half, and the OpenAI model takes a red coin every round.
Over four model generations, the Google model's record fills with more green each time and the OpenAI model's with less, ending at none.
After nine fast rounds, a coral frame marks the last round: the Anthropic model still hands its coin over, and the Google model, green for nine rounds, takes it.

title: Data quality across ten online research platforms
beats: Respondents walk out of ten doorways in four groups (direct panels, hybrid networks, marketplaces, MTurk), and each finished survey lands on the board.
A detector gate switches on and exposes two MTurk respondents as robots, which drop into a short tally. No other platform has any.

A coral lens reads every answer: nearly all direct-panel answers turn green, fewer from hybrid networks, about half from marketplaces, few from MTurk. The careless answers make a tally far longer than the bot tally.
Coins pay for one usable answer on each kind of platform; the direct panels need the fewest coins.

title: Vertical tacit collusion
beats: On an honest ranked list, the shopper's AI drone reads from the top and brings back product A, the best and cheapest.
The platform's crane lifts the pricier product B to the top, but B's plain page does not convince the drone, which still buys A. A small harm bar appears.
The seller dresses up B's page while B sits low on the list. The page tugs the drone, it still buys A, and a second harm bar appears.

With a wall between the platform and the seller, the dressed-up B sits on top and the drone buys it. The coins go to the seller and the platform, and the joint harm bar rises past the two separate bars stacked together.

title: Constructive choice
beats: Two shoppers with an accuracy goal (the teal target). On the easy screen the shopper opens nine option cards; on the hard screen, where each card is strong on one bar and weak on another, the shopper stops at five.
Both now want to save effort (the gold hourglass). On the easy screen the shopper stops at four; on the hard screen the shopper keeps clicking up to nine.
Both screens fill with fifty small options and the target joins the hourglass: now both goals are in mind.
With both goals in mind, the hard screen gets the shorter search: five cards on the easy screen, three on the hard one.

title: The Importance of Advertising Skepticism for Brand Extension Appeals
beats: A computer brand's ad shows a printer, a close extension. The brand's claim flows into it and on to a trusting viewer and a skeptic with a magnifying glass; both hearts fill.
The ad shows sunglasses, a distant extension. The claim fades before it arrives and neither heart fills.

The ad shows an espresso machine, a moderately similar extension. The trusting viewer's heart fills, but at the skeptic's lens the claim stops, the lens flashes red, and the skeptic's heart stays empty.
The espresso machine gains the computer's screen, a feature it shares with the brand's products. The claim passes the lens and the skeptic's heart fills.

title: The space commons
beats: Teal and violet rockets launch from Earth. Each new satellite sends a gold star to its operator's bar on the leaderboard, and the orbit fills up.
The violet operator fires a missile at its own dead satellite. The blast earns a star, but red debris spreads around the orbit, breaks a teal satellite, and the space station flashes red.

A coral frame turns the leaderboard into a public ranking. The blast star turns red and falls off, the dead satellites burn up in the atmosphere, each disposal earns a star, and the debris falls away.
The clean orbit turns green and both bars stand level.

kind: Journal article (new story; was a noise animation)
title: Consumer responses to infectious disease cues
beats: A normal trip: the shopper eats a free sample, takes the new violet product, waits right behind another shopper, and drops a coin in the charity jar.
A second trip: the customer in line sneezes. In the thought bubble the face turns to disgust, the eye narrows, and the heart becomes a shield.
Choices that have nothing to do with germs change: the shopper leans away from the samples, takes the familiar gold brand, waits far back in the queue, and keeps the coin.
